rarefy

RAIR-uh-fye · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To rarefy is to make rare, thin, or less dense.

The lab uses a special chamber to rarefy the air before the experiment begins.

Worked Example

As balloons rise higher, the surrounding atmosphere continues to rarefy around them.

The air isn't disappearing -- its particles are simply spreading farther apart and becoming less dense, which is exactly rarefy.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

thin: To thin something is the everyday way to make it less dense — a cook thins a sauce, a crowd thins out after a game. Rarefy is the precise, scientific-sounding word for the same idea, used above all for air and gases growing less dense.

dilute: To dilute is to weaken a liquid by mixing something extra into it — watering down juice. Rarefy works the opposite way: nothing is added; the same particles simply spread farther apart until the gas is less dense.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

compress: press something into a smaller, denser space

Where it sits · how low the density drops — spread out → rarefy → vacuum

spread out vs. rarefy: Spreading out simply covers more area; rarefying specifically means the particles themselves become less densely packed.

vacuum vs. rarefy: A rarefied atmosphere still has some particles present, just widely spaced; a true vacuum has essentially none at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — rar

prefix — rar: thin, uncommon (Latin (rarus))

suffix — -efy

suffix — -efy: to make or cause to become (Latin (-ficare))

Put it together

Put it together: Rarefy comes from Latin rarus ('thin, uncommon') + -ficare ('to make') -- literally 'to make thin.'

Use the root in a new word: rare

Use the root in a new word: rare: The same rarus root gives us the everyday word rare, describing something uncommon or thinly spread.

Word Choice

Rarefy is most often used for gases and atmospheres becoming thinner at altitude, though it can also describe anything non-literally thinned out or made more elite, as in "rarefied social circles."
